headline: AI in job market creates infinite doom loop for applicants and employers
summary: Job seekers use AI to optimize applications for AI-powered Applicant Tracking Systems, while employers use AI to screen identical applications. This creates a "doom loop" of escalating AI use and mistrust for both sides.
details: Job seekers are increasingly optimizing their resumes for AI-powered Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS). One job seeker found her resume was dinged for minor formatting issues, highlighting the rigid requirements of these systems. This forces candidates to tailor applications with specific keywords and formats to pass initial automated screenings.

Tools like Jobscan promise to help applicants game these systems, operating on the belief that only the top 10-20% of AI-ranked candidates are seen by humans. This creates immense pressure for job seekers to conform to what they believe the AI wants.

However, this premise isn't always correct. While some organizations use automated ranking, many still rely on human review from start to finish. The functionality of ATS varies significantly, and whether AI is used depends on the specific product and features a company pays for.

Daniel Chait, CEO of ATS company Greenhouse, describes this as an "AI doom loop." Both job seekers and employers are using AI to solve their problems, but in ways that exacerbate the overall issue, leading to more AI use without clear benefit.

This escalating use of AI by both sides is creating a breakdown of trust in the job market. Candidates spend significant time optimizing applications only to hear nothing, while employers receive hundreds of near-identical, AI-generated applications.

Recruiters and HR managers are divided on AI use; some automate screening, others don't. Companies like Toshiba emphasize human review, while others, like Doist, found ATS rankings unhelpful in experiments. Unwanted AI use is also appearing in interview stages, with candidates using AI for real-time answers.
